chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
title: Which schools to attend: Berklee, North Texas, Eastman
summary: Herman recommends Berklee, North Texas, New England Conservatory or Eastman for brass, and cites Birch Johnson's path from Alabama to Eastman.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: If you had to plan a curriculum or something and help somebody, what are some of those most important things you feel should be in the jazz education curriculum? You've had all these players in your --
You mean, from an education point --
Yeah. I mean, what are they missing? Is there something missing -- what are those things that you think are absolutely indispensable?
Well, in the first place, if you're starting to play young, you better go to either Berklee, North
-- New England Conservatory. If you're a brass player particularly, you should consider going to Eastman, if you can get in.

But then, we have so many great music departments in state universities all over this country, that really, you're not limited. It just depends on where you want to finish up. Like, I think a great example is Birch Johnson in our band, who got his degree at the University of Alabama, and then went to Eastman and got his master's. That I think is a wise decision.
And it didn't take that long, nor was it that difficult, because he had the ability and he had the training. It was just a question of improving it.
Well, I was thinking that those elements in their training, what -- you might evaluate as really key things that those universities and those schools should include. That's what I was thinking about.

Well, I think that you'll find that most departments at this point are pretty complete. And if a young person makes sensible, good inquiries, and delves -- or asks what's available and what he expects or doesn't expect, he can make a clearcut decision as to which music department he should attend.
